analysis.one_liner: Bars federal energy regulators from counting the climate damage of carbon emissions when weighing rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal agencies calculate a dollar figure — the "social cost of carbon" — for how much each ton of carbon dioxide or methane pollution costs society, and use that number to justify climate rules. This bill would forbid the Department of Energy and the EPA from using that number in any cost-benefit analysis, rule, or guidance unless Congress passed a separate law allowing it. It would also require the EPA to report how often the metric has been used since 2009.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, oil, gas, and coal producers would have gained, because the social cost of greenhouse gases is the tool agencies use to show that the benefits of limiting emissions outweigh the compliance costs. Removing it makes climate and methane rules harder to defend in court and in cost-benefit reviews.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the Energy Secretary and the EPA Administrator from considering the social cost of carbon, methane, nitrous oxide, or any other greenhouse gas in cost-benefit analyses under any law or executive order, in rulemakings, in guidance, or as a justification for any agency action [S3].
The only exception would be if Congress later enacted a law explicitly authorizing agencies to consider those social costs [S3].

The bill's findings argue the metric was developed without following the Office of Management and Budget's discount-rate guidance, was never peer-reviewed with public comment, and that the regulations it justifies cost American families billions of dollars each year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the costs of carbon and methane pollution — worse heat waves, storms, crop losses, and health damage — would have remained outside the government's official accounting, tilting future regulatory decisions toward cheaper-to-pollute energy producers. Households would bear those uncounted climate damages.

drawbacks.text: Supporters argued in good faith that the social cost estimates deviated from the 3 and 7 percent discount rates prescribed by OMB's Circular A-4 and counted global rather than domestic benefits, making the numbers looser than the government's own cost-benefit rules require [S3].
The bill singles out one analytical input rather than reforming the cost-benefit process as a whole, so other contested assumptions in regulatory analysis would have remained untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real criticism — that the social cost of greenhouse gases was developed by an interagency working group without the notice, comment, and discount-rate discipline OMB's guidance calls for [S3]. But its remedy is blunt: it would ban the metric outright rather than require agencies to redo it under proper methodology, and the practical effect would be to strip climate damages out of the government's decision-making entirely. Compliance savings for fossil fuel producers would come at the cost of officially ignoring harms that fall on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in December 2016, referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, and the committee never acted before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Lankford introduced the bill on December 6, 2016, in the final month of the 114th Congress [S1].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day; no further action was taken [S5].
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill died in committee without ever reaching the floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the EPA and Department of Energy kept their ability to weigh climate damages in cost-benefit analyses, and the oil and gas methane rules the bill targeted stayed on the books for the moment. Fossil fuel producers did not get the analytical tool they opposed removed; climate and public-health advocates kept the status quo.

for.name: James Lankford
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, a one-senator introduction with no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: James Inhofe
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never scheduled action on the bill during the final weeks of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, and its only support was a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors, so no party-line pattern can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill was aimed squarely at EPA methane rules for the oil and gas sector, which relied on the social cost of methane to show their benefits outweighed compliance costs [S3]. Banning the metric would have made those rules harder to justify, saving producers money while leaving methane pollution costs with the public.

The bill's findings frame the social cost of carbon as a tool used to regulate coal out of the energy mix [S3]. Removing it would have weakened the cost-benefit case for carbon limits on coal plants, at the expense of air-quality and climate benefits for everyone else.
